title: Appendix A — Symbolic Action in a Poem by Keats

outline.section: Opening frame: Ode as viaticum to oracle (book p. 447)
outline.summary: Burke announces the analytic project — to read Keats's 'Ode on a Grecian Urn' dramatistically, treating the poem as a viaticum (sacramental provision-for-the-journey) leading by a series of transformations to the oracular closing identity 'Beauty is truth, truth beauty.' He distinguishes language-as-information (epistemological / scientific) from language-as-action (poetic / symbolic), grounding the entire essay's method: 'a poem is an act, the symbolic act of the poet who made it.' The romantic dialectic of beauty vs. truth (aesthetic vs. practical) is identified as the motivational pressure the Ode must transcend. Burke notes the oracle could not have been uttered in stanza I; the five stanzas of transformation are required for romanticism to transcend itself through romanticism.

outline.section: Stanza I — apostrophe and rhetorical questions (book pp. 448-449)
outline.summary: Burke reads the periodic opening sentence as transmuting from address to breathless interrogation. The stanza's hesitation between 'deities or mortals' supplies a 'bare hint' of two motivational levels (divine / human) that the Ode will progressively differentiate. The figures on the urn — sylvan-historian addressee, deities-or-mortals, maidens-loth, mad-pursuit — are pentadic agents whose acts the urn arrests in a scene of frozen-time.

outline.section: Stanza II — mystic oxymoron, unheard melodies, arrested pre-ecstasy (book pp. 449-450)
outline.summary: The 'heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard are sweeter' formula deploys mystic oxymoron — Burke's technical name for the rhetorical figure in which an epithet of contrary significance is joined to its noun (cruel kindness, laborious idleness). Inaudible sound functions as motives-behind-motives, paralleled to the prime-mover-at-rest, the principle of sweetness that has transcended sweetness, the sub-atomic particles devoid of temperature. Contrast with Shelley's naturalistic-temporal retrospection establishes Keats's form-of-thought as mystical (eternal present) rather than temporal. The erotic suspension — 'Bold Lover, never canst thou kiss / Though winning near the goal' — is read not as arrested ecstasy but as arrested pre-ecstasy.

outline.section: Stanza II expanded — biographical / cultural motives, love-death equation (book pp. 450-452)
outline.summary: Burke adds knowledge of Keats's tubercular illness and 19th-century romanticism as motivational substrates. The phthisic fever supplies a 'constitutional substrate' such that fever and chill are modes of one illness (a sub-pentadic substance-claim). The love-death equation typical of romanticism (musically monumentalized in the Wagnerian Liebestod) is shown to be over-determined by capitalist-individualist property-structure: heightened individual identity makes union-as-death more imperious. Burke cites Shakespeare's 'The Phoenix and the Turtle' on property thus 'appall'd' and Keats's letter to Fanny Brawne on fire/burning. Methodological aside: the poet's body is patient, his mind is agent; the Aristotelian action/passion grammar is recapitulated through the Christian acta/passiones paradox (martyr-act = martyr-passion) and secularized in romantic creativeness as bodily suffering redeemed by poetic act.

outline.section: Stanza III — the fulcrum: action splits from passion (book pp. 452-453)
outline.summary: Stanza III is the central stanza, 'properly the fulcrum of [the Ode's] swing.' The 'happy, happy boughs' / 'happy melodist' / 'more happy love' refrain enacts the definitive division: transcendental fever (felicitous, above 'all breathing human passion') splits from earthly fever ('a burning forehead, and a parching tongue'). The malign bodily passion is left behind; a wholly benign spiritual activity has split off. Burke names this the completion of one curve and identifies the next required movement: scene must be brought up to match the now-transcendent act.

outline.section: Methodological interlude — the scene-act ratio as prediction-engine (book pp. 453-456)
outline.summary: Burke explicitly invokes the scene-act ratio: 'the quality of the act shares the quality of the scene in which it is enacted (the synecdochic relation of container and thing contained).' He generalizes via supernatural cosmogonies (humans take on attributes of gods when acting in cosmic scenes imbued with godhead) and via the theological controversy whether God willed the good because it is good, or the good is good because God willed it. The first formula is dramatically more symmetrical, because 'because' assigns God a kind of scene (objective goodness as ground); the pun on 'ground' (place / cause) is leveraged. Scholastic 'pure act' for God is glossed as itself the ultimate scene of human acting. Citing Leo Spitzer on milieu/ambiance and Coleridge on poetic action as 'dim analogue of Creation,' Burke prophesies post eventum that stanza IV will concretize a transcendent scene matching the transcendent act.

outline.section: Stanza IV — the deathy-deathless scene; sacrifice imagery (book pp. 455-457)
outline.summary: 'Who are these coming to the sacrifice? / To what green altar, O mysterious priest...' The fourth stanza concretizes the transcendent scene: green altar, garlanded heifer, little town emptied for evermore. Burke reads the vision as 'death' or 'immortality' equivalently — immortality is the 'good word' for death and must be conceived in terms of death (Donne: 'I / Am, by being dead, immortall'). The sacrificial imagery is communication-with-the-immortal-or-dead. Technical observation: the return of rhetorical questions in stanza IV preserves continuity with stanza I as 'unheard tonal felicity,' making us feel exclamations of II/III had been questions all along. Footnote on imagery's logic: imagery has no negation — 'this, not that' is unavailable; only 'this and that,' 'this-that' (a commandment is latently a provocation). Burke parallels stanza IV to the sestet of Keats's 'On First Looking Into Chapman's Homer' — both 'come upon a scene,' both end on silence ('not a soul can tell' ↔ 'wild surmise').

Burke states the unit's load-bearing pentadic chiasmus: 'The scene on the Urn is really the scene behind the Urn; the Urn is literally the ground of this scene, but transcendentally the scene is the ground of the Urn. The Urn contains the scene out of which it arose.' This is a worked instance of container-thing-contained inversion (the methodological move from GM-01) operating dialectically within a single artifact. Burke aligns the poem's dialectical progression — human → divine → ground-of-the-divine — with the theological speculation about grounds-for-God's-creative-act treated in the methodological interlude.

outline.section: Stanza V — Cold Pastoral and the oracle (book pp. 458-461)
outline.summary: 'O Attic shape! Fair attitude!' — Burke seizes the Urn's designation as 'Attitude' as the key terminological coincidence: 'an attitude is an arrested, or incipient act — not just an object, or thing.' The 'Cold Pastoral!' marks the move from transcendental fever to transcendental chill (paralleling the body's phthisic fever-to-chill); but since bodily passion has dropped out, the chill is wholly benign. The wordplay 'brede / breed' and 'overwrought / excited' merges sexuality and craftsmanship. The closing oracle 'Beauty is truth, truth beauty' is achieved at a level where earthly contradictions no longer prevail — solving the romantic split (poetry/science, aesthetic/practical) by translating it into the dramatistic grammar.

outline.section: Conceptual translation: 'Act is scene, scene act' (book pp. 459-460)
outline.summary: Burke offers the dramatistic gloss as a parallel transformation to the Ode's imagistic transformation: substitute 'poetry' for 'beauty' (then 'act' for 'poetry'), and 'science' for 'truth' (then 'scene' for 'science'). The chain — beauty=poetry=act, truth=science=scene — yields the grammatical oracle 'Act is scene, scene act.' Beauty=act because beauty is an assertion, affirmation, creation. Truth/science=scene because science is knowledge-of-what-is and the over-all universal scene is what-is. Burke immediately breaks the symmetry: idealism (romanticism) features Agent, not Act; the Urn is properly an 'attitude,' which is incipient act, the property of an agent. Keats personifies the Urn — 'beauty was not so much the act of an agent as the act of an agent.'

outline.section: Yeats parallel: extending the Keatsian identification (book pp. 460-461)
outline.summary: Burke imports two Yeats passages. From the Byzantium poems: 'Once out of nature I shall never take / My bodily form from any natural thing, / But such a form as Grecian goldsmiths make' — extending Keats's Urn-identification one step (immortality as fabricated golden bird). From 'Among School Children': 'O chestnut tree, great rooted blossomer / Are you the leaf, the blossom or the bole? / O body swayed to music, O brightening glance, / How can we know the dancer from the dance?' Burke reads the chestnut as personified agent grounding scenic manifestations; dancer-dance merger makes the agent 'foremost among the equals' even when act + scene + agent commingle. Both Yeats and Keats are exceptional among romantics in being properly dramatistic, where the typical romantic translates scene-into-agent (materialist science conversely translating agent-into-scene).

outline.section: Review and contrast with Kretschmer (book pp. 461-463)
outline.summary: Burke recapitulates the four-movement curve: ambiguous fever → fever splits → action transcends passion → transcendent act requires transcendent scene. He contrasts his analysis with a Kretschmer-school materialist explanation that would treat disease-as-cause / poem-as-effect — making the mental action a 'mere epiphenomenon' or 'symptom of the disease.' This reductive Scene→Act translation (the materialist mirror of romantic Scene→Agent) misses 'the essential matter here, the intense linguistic activity.' The Ode's symbolic action is irreducible to either pole; dramatism preserves the act's standing as act.

concepts.label: Viaticum (poem as)
concepts.gloss: Sacramental provision-for-the-journey; Burke's frame for the Ode as transformation-vehicle leading from doubt through stages to the oracular truth-beauty identity.

concepts.label: Symbolic action
concepts.gloss: Language considered as a mode of action (poetic) rather than information (scientific); a poem is the symbolic act of its maker, which the reader re-enacts in reading.

concepts.label: The oracle (Beauty is truth)
concepts.gloss: The closing identity 'Beauty is truth, truth beauty'; achievable only after five stanzas of transformation because it resolves a romantic dialectical opposition (aesthetic vs. practical) that must first be raised to a transcendent level.

concepts.label: Mystic oxymoron
concepts.gloss: The rhetorical figure in which an epithet of contrary significance is added to a word (cruel kindness, laborious idleness, unheard melody); a mark of motives-behind-motives, the prime-mover-at-rest paradox.

concepts.label: Scene-act ratio (dramatic ratio)
concepts.gloss: Law of dramatic consistency whereby the quality of the act shares the quality of the scene in which it is enacted; the synecdochic relation of container and thing contained. Burke names this explicitly in the Keats essay and uses it as a prediction-engine for stanza IV.

concepts.label: Transcendent act
concepts.gloss: The spiritual activity that splits off from bodily passion at the end of stanza III; once transcendent, it requires a scene of like quality, generating the demand stanza IV will meet.

concepts.label: Transcendent scene
concepts.gloss: The deathy-deathless ground summoned by the scene-act ratio to match the transcendent act; concretized in stanza IV as the sacrificial-procession / little-town vision.

concepts.label: Ground (pun: place / cause)
concepts.gloss: The pun in 'ground' linking place and cause; Burke leverages it to align scene-as-locus with scene-as-reason in the theological 'because' that gives God's act its scene.

concepts.label: Urn / scene container-inversion
concepts.gloss: 'The Urn is literally the ground of this scene, but transcendentally the scene is the ground of the Urn.' A dramatistic inversion of container and thing-contained within a single artifact.

concepts.label: Attitude (incipient or arrested act)
concepts.gloss: Keats's designation 'Fair attitude!' read as terminologically perfect: an attitude is an arrested, or incipient act — not an object. This terminological coincidence becomes load-bearing for Burke's later sixth-pentad-term addition (Rhetoric of Motives, 1950).

concepts.label: Incipient act
concepts.gloss: Acts in a state of arrest just prior to fulfilment (the Bold Lover, the heifer led to altar, the depicted figures); related to but distinguishable from arrested act.

concepts.label: Arrested pre-ecstasy
concepts.gloss: Burke's correction of 'arrested ecstasy': the urn's lovers are suspended just-prior-to-fulfilment, an eternal prolongation; cited via G. Wilson Knight's 'tiptoe' effect.

concepts.label: Love-death equation
concepts.gloss: Romantic identification of consummated love with death (Liebestod); over-determined by capitalist individualism's heightening of individual identity, which makes union-as-death imperative; corroborated by Keats's Fanny Brawne letters and Shakespeare's Phoenix and the Turtle.

concepts.label: Agent/patient ↔ action/passion grammar
concepts.gloss: Aristotelian reciprocal: action/passion; in Christian inversion (acta = passiones of martyrs), patience becomes a property of moral agent; secularized in romanticism as bodily suffering redeemed by poetic act.

concepts.label: Constitutional substrate (illness)
concepts.gloss: Burke's substance-claim: phthisic fever and phthisic chill are modes of one underlying illness; this same substance-logic governs the Ode's transcendental fever-then-chill arc.

concepts.label: Fever→chill transformation
concepts.gloss: The Ode moves from heat (stanza III: panting, for ever warm; bodily: burning forehead, parching tongue) to cold (stanza V: Cold Pastoral); benign because bodily passion has dropped out.

concepts.label: Deathy-deathless scene
concepts.gloss: Burke's coinage for the immortal-conceived-through-death; the Urn as 'an immortal act in a mortal scene' that was 'originally an immortal act in a mortal scene quite different.'

concepts.label: Imagery has no negation
concepts.gloss: Logical 'this, not that' is unavailable to imagery, which can only say 'this and that' / 'this-that'; a commandment is latently a provocation. A small but load-bearing principle for symbolic-action analysis.

concepts.label: Act is scene, scene act (dramatistic translation)
concepts.gloss: Burke's purely-grammatical parallel of the Ode's oracle: beauty=poetry=act and truth=science=scene, yielding 'Act is scene, scene act.' Immediately broken by the recognition that idealism features Agent, making the Urn an attitude (act-of-an-agent).

concepts.label: Romantic philosophy (idealism featuring Agent)
concepts.gloss: Burke locates Keats / Yeats / romantic poetics in the Agent-featuring philosophic family; ordinary romantic translation is scene→agent (the materialist mirror is agent→scene).

concepts.label: Re-enactment (reader's symbolic act)
concepts.gloss: The poem as object enables readers to re-enact it; the viaticum carries readers into the quality of the scene the Urn depicts.

concepts.label: Intense linguistic activity (vs. epiphenomenalism)
concepts.gloss: Burke's final pivot against Kretschmer-style materialism: treating the poem as symptom-of-disease misses the essential matter — the intense linguistic activity that is the symbolic act itself.

concepts.label: Applied dramatism on a lyric
concepts.gloss: The methodological template: deploying pentad terms + ratios + substance-logic + dialectical-transformation on a single short lyric, with continuous attention to its imagistic and biographical levels.

the scene 'behind' the Urn — transcendentally the ground of the Urn itself

agent_identifications.agent: the speaker / poet addressing the urn
deities-or-mortals, Bold Lover, fair youth, mysterious priest, marble men and maidens
Keats himself — body as patient, mind as agent

agency_identifications.agency: music / piping ('soft pipes, play on') as agency of address
language as mode of action — symbolic action as the agency
the urn's visual surface (sculpted figures) as agency through which the dead world communicates

purpose_identifications.purpose: the oracular identity 'Beauty is truth, truth beauty' as ultimate purpose
transcendence of the romantic split (aesthetic/practical, beauty/truth)
redemption of bodily suffering by poetic act (Christian-romantic secularized)

ratios_deployed.instance: Burke explicitly invokes this ratio as the prediction-engine that demands stanza IV: the transcendent act of stanza III requires a transcendent scene to match it (book p. 454: 'the quality of the act shares the quality of the scene in which it is enacted').
The urn-as-scene determines the agents depicted on it; biographically, the romantic-capitalist scene shapes the agent's love-death-fixated imagining.
The symbolic act of the poem culminates in the oracular truth-beauty identity as its purpose.
Christian-romantic inversion: the moral agent's patience becomes itself an act (martyr-acta = martyr-passiones); Keats's mind-as-agent uses bodily-passion-as-act-material.
Imagery's logic ('no negation') is a scenic constraint on the agency-of-imagery — only 'this and that' is available, not 'this, not that'.

symbolic_action_transformations.summary: Periodic-to-breathless transmutation in stanza I — periodic structure dissolved into rhetorical questions, opening the motivational hesitation between divine and human.
Mystic oxymoron in stanza II — heard sound surpassed by unheard sound, ear surpassed by spirit, establishing motives-behind-motives.
Erotic suspension as arrested pre-ecstasy — eternal prolongation of the moment just prior to fulfilment.
Stanza III fulcrum — the fever splits; benign spiritual activity (action) parts from malign bodily fever (passion).
Scene-act demand satisfied in stanza IV — transcendent act receives its transcendent scene (sacrificial vision, deathy-deathless ground).
Container-thing-contained inversion — Urn becomes scene's ground literally; scene becomes Urn's ground transcendentally.
Fever-to-chill modulation in stanza V — bodily passion dropped, chill is wholly benign; 'Cold Pastoral!' as marmorean utterance.
Oracle delivered — at this transcendent level the romantic split is resolved; 'Beauty is truth, truth beauty.'
Burke's conceptual parallel — 'Act is scene, scene act' as the purely-grammatical equivalent, immediately corrected to 'act of an agent' via the Urn-as-Attitude (the romantic-idealist Agent-feature).

applied_pentad_demonstration.methodological_template_for_dissertation: GM-10 demonstrates the workflow of dramatistic single-text analysis: (i) state the explicit framing claim about the text's terminal motive-statement (the oracle); (ii) walk the text segment by segment with continuous identification of pentad terms in their imagistic embodiments; (iii) detect a structural fulcrum (the splitting of one term-cluster from another); (iv) deploy the scene-act ratio (or whichever ratio is foregrounded) as a prediction-engine for the next segment; (v) thicken biographical and cultural-historical motives without letting them reduce the symbolic act to epiphenomenon; (vi) recognize sub-pentadic substance-claims (here: the phthisic-fever-and-chill as modes of one illness substance) that re-cross with the text's transformations; (vii) terminate with a conceptual translation that exhibits the dramatistic grammar underlying the text's imagistic resolution; (viii) refuse reductive materialist alternatives that would treat the symbolic act as symptom. The dissertation's empirical-adaptation chapter at single-text scale (a single game-text, a single user-trajectory) inherits steps (i)-(viii) directly.

positions.claim: A poem must be read as symbolic act — language-as-mode-of-action — not as language-as-information; the reader re-enacts the poet's symbolic act.
positions.stake: Forecloses purely semantic / referential / epistemic criticism; commits the analyst to motivational rather than denotational reading. Foundational for the dramatistic method as such.

positions.claim: The scene-act ratio is not merely a descriptive observation but a predictive law: once a transcendent act has been generated, the text MUST (if well-formed) generate a scene of corresponding quality.
positions.stake: Promotes dramatism from terminology to compositional law; supplies the analyst with a prediction-engine for what the text will do next. Methodologically the single most generative move in the essay.

positions.claim: The Urn's designation 'Attitude' is terminologically perfect for symbolic action: an attitude is an arrested or incipient act, the property of an agent — not an object.
positions.stake: Anticipates Burke's later promotion of Attitude to a sixth pentad term in A Rhetoric of Motives (1950); marks the Agent-feature of romantic/idealist poetics; reorients the analyst from object-criticism toward act-criticism.

positions.claim: Reductive materialist accounts (Kretschmer-school) that treat disease-as-cause and poem-as-effect, making the mental action an epiphenomenon of bodily passion, miss the essential matter — the intense linguistic activity that constitutes the symbolic act.
positions.stake: Defends the irreducibility of symbolic action against the materialist mirror-image of the very romantic translation Burke has been analyzing. Methodologically critical: dramatism is anti-reductive on both sides.

positions.claim: The Ode performs an abolishing of romanticism through romanticism — the five stanzas of transformation are required for the romantic philosophy to transcend itself by raising its own dialectic to a higher order.
positions.stake: Frames the Ode as self-reflexive at the level of philosophic idiom; allows a romantic poem to be read as a critique of romanticism without ceasing to be romantic.

positions.claim: Imagery cannot say 'this, not that'; it can only say 'this and that' or 'this-that'. Hence imagistic transformation operates by amalgamation, not by negation.
positions.stake: Constrains the analyst's account of how poems do dialectic — they cannot simply oppose; they must merge, transcend, or split. A small but load-bearing principle for symbolic-action analysis.

tensions.claim_a: The dramatistic translation of the Ode's oracle yields 'Act is scene, scene act' (Beauty=Act, Truth=Scene).
tensions.claim_b: But idealism / romanticism features Agent, not Act; the Urn is properly an 'attitude' (incipient act, property of an agent); so the romantic-idealist version is 'beauty is the act of an agent.'
tensions.burke_resolution: Burke does not resolve so much as acknowledge: 'I must break the symmetry a little.' The dramatistic grammar generates the cleaner 'Act is scene, scene act' formula; the philosophic idiom of the Ode (romantic idealism) introduces the Agent-feature that breaks the symmetry. Both readings are simultaneously valid at different levels (grammar of motives vs. idiom of motives).
tensions.dissertation_relevance: The Burke pipeline's deepest tension: dramatistic grammar is universal at the expression-level, but particular philosophies feature different terms — and any given text exhibits both layers at once. Operationalization Manual Section A must record this duality for every pentad term.

tensions.claim_a: Burke insists on the irreducibility of symbolic action — the poem is not an epiphenomenon of bodily disease; the Kretschmer-school reduction misses the intense linguistic activity (book p. 463).
tensions.claim_b: Yet Burke himself spends multiple pages correlating the Ode's fever-to-chill arc with Keats's phthisic fever-and-chill, using the constitutional substrate of the illness as a substance-claim that grounds the text's transformations (book pp. 452, 458).
tensions.burke_resolution: Burke's discipline is correlation-without-reduction: biographical and bodily motives are real and analytically usable, but they are co-active substrates not causal grounds. The mind-as-agent uses the body-as-patient (the Aristotelian-Christian-romantic chain). The dramatistic analysis must mention both without subordinating the symbolic act to the bodily symptom.
tensions.dissertation_relevance: This tension licenses (for the dissertation) the use of behavioral / biometric / situational data as motivational substrate without reduction — a critical move for game-user motivation studies that want to use telemetry without becoming behaviorist.

tensions.claim_a: Imagery cannot say 'this, not that'; it can only say 'this and that' or 'this-that' (book p. 456 fn).
tensions.claim_b: Yet the Ode is structured as a dialectical progression of splittings — fever splits from chill, action splits from passion, transcendent from bodily — operations that look like 'this, not that' on the conceptual plane.
tensions.burke_resolution: The splittings Burke detects are not negations but separations-by-amalgamation-then-transcendence: the fever-and-chill remain modes of one illness (the substance is preserved), the transcendent act remains in relation to (transcending, leaving) the bodily passion. Imagistic dialectic operates by progressive raising of the joint-term to a new level, never by simple opposition.

methodological_template_summary: GM-10 IS the dissertation's empirical-adaptation template at single-text scale, paralleling the role of Calleja's Appendix in the In-Game pipeline. The procedure is: (1) state the text's terminal motive-statement (oracle / thesis-claim / game-end-state); (2) read the text segment by segment with continuous pentad-tagging at the imagistic level; (3) detect structural fulcra where pentad-clusters split or combine; (4) deploy the most-foregrounded ratio as a prediction-engine for the next segment; (5) add biographical / cultural / historical motives as substrates without reducing the symbolic act; (6) recognize sub-pentadic substance-claims (illness, property-structure, philosophic idiom) that re-cross with the text's transformations; (7) end with a conceptual translation that exhibits the dramatistic grammar underlying the imagistic resolution; (8) refuse reductive alternatives that would epiphenomenalize the symbolic act.
